newsitem.title: UK: Russian gold mines need better investment climate.
newsitem.headline: Russian gold mines need better investment climate.

text.p: Political uncertainties, legal complexities and high taxes are hampering a badly needed influx of foreign capital to support the gold and diamond mining industry in the former Soviet Union.

Speakers at a conference here stressed on Wednesday that the investment climate needs drastic improvement to arouse substantial interest from western banks and drum up the hundreds of millions of dollars needed to keep the mining industry going.

"There is absolutely no doubt that the development of the gold market and the mining and refining industry substantially depends on foreign investment," said Aleksandr Potemkin, deputy chairman and director of foreign operations at the central bank of Russia.

"But before we can expect active participation we have to develop proper and transparent conditions," he told the conference on the mining and and processing of gold and diamonds in the Confederation of Independent States.

So far most of the foreign money has come from junior exploration firms, but much bigger investments from major players are needed in the gold and diamond industry -- not only for new developments, but also to maintain current production levels.

"Finance remains the key," said Raj Kohli, associate director of Banque Paribas in Britain. "But for the big money, you need involvement of the seniors," he told an audience of consultants, bankers and mining executives.
Evgeny Bychkov, president of the Russian Association of Diamond Manufacturers, said the diamond industry requires investments of about $200 million a year in the near future.

"The diamond-rich provinces of Russia are at present financially unable to carry out large-scale development work and are accordingly interested in attracting inward investment," he said. "I would like to say that you (western companies) are extremely welcome (to invest)."

Diamond producer Almazy-Rossii Sakha (ARS), which mines over 95 percent of Russian stones, in July gave London investment bank NatWest Markets a mandate to raise $500 million to increase exploration and production.
Russia is the world's second largest diamond producer and also ranks among the world's biggest gold mining countries.
The problem for the gold mining industry is that it has to switch to hard rock mining, requiring big investments in modern technologies, as alluvial reserves are getting depleted.

The sheer size of the gold and diamond resources in the former Soviet Union could spur mining fever in the early 1990s, but enthusiasm among western firms to start digging has cooled in recent years, said Kohli.
"Early optimism is replaced by sober realism," he said, warning that only the prospect of above average returns could attract the attention of big mining firms.
But with improved legislation, political commitment and a couple of success stories, countries such as Russia and Kazakhstan could attract the money needed, Kohli said.
"We need "good news' stories. You require projects to come onstream on budget; not over budget. Once you get these kind of stories in place, you are going to get the ball rolling."
